library: Taylor EOS Day-in-the-Life — Inventory, Warehouse, Purchasing, Scanner

authority_model.summary: Inventory authority is a THREE-GATE system, not a single active:false switch. Read this before interpreting any PERMISSION_DENIAL activity in this library.

gates.name: catalog activation
gates.rule: A capability registered active:false in functions/src/access/permissionCatalog.ts denies unconditionally for every principal, AHEAD of any Role grant.
gates.evidence: functions/src/access/resolveEffectivePermission.ts:264-265 — CURRENT: if (permission.active === false && !input.activationOverrides?.has(input.permissionId)) return { decision: 'DENY', reason: 'inactivePermission' };

gates.name: per-environment activation override
gates.rule: An environment MAY lift the gate-1 deny for named ids. platform-sandbox DOES so for the whole inventory set. Production carries no such key and is triple-blocked; role-keyed resolution returns EMPTY for production regardless of data, and a test asserts it.
gates.evidence: config/environments.json:106-128 — CURRENT: platform-sandbox activates inventory.catalog.read, inventory.serializedAsset.read/.acquire, inventory.location.display.read, inventory.transfer.create/.dispatch/.receive/.cancel, inventory.cycleCount.create/.submit/.reconcile/.cancel, inventory.catalog.alias.read, inventory.balance.read, inventory.location.bin.manage/.read, inventory.placement.record, inventory.stock.relocate, inventory.returns.intake. functions/src/access/environmentCapabilityOverrides.ts:183-215,505-540 — CURRENT: the in-bundle snapshot, drift-guarded against that file. config/environments.json:225-227 — CURRENT: the certification emulator activates ONLY inventory.cycleCount.create/.submit/.reconcile (cancel deliberately excluded).

gates.name: qualifying Role grant
gates.rule: ACTIVATION IS NOT A GRANT. After gates 1 and 2, a principal still needs a qualifying Role grant or resolution returns DENY noQualifyingGrant. Declaring a Role grants nothing; a principal holds it only via a governed, audited roleAssignment.
gates.evidence: functions/src/access/governedBusinessRoles.ts:1239-1250 — CURRENT: INVENTORY_PUT_AWAY_OPERATOR_ROLE declares exactly inventory.location.bin.read and inventory.placement.record and states 'Declaring it grants nothing.' functions/src/access/environmentCapabilityOverrides.ts:526-528 — CURRENT: 'ACTIVATION IS NOT A GRANT: a principal without inventoryStockRelocationOperator (or admin/owner by derivation) still resolves DENY.'

authority_model.correction_to_lane_brief: The lane brief stated that every bin/placement/relocate capability is active:false and 'granted to no Role', so screens exist over authority nobody holds. VERIFIED AND REFINED: the active:false registrations are real and were confirmed. But (a) a Role DOES declare the put-away pair (INVENTORY_PUT_AWAY_OPERATOR_ROLE), and a separate inventoryStockRelocationOperator Role is named for relocation; and (b) platform-sandbox carries a governed per-environment activation override for the entire inventory set, so in the sandbox the gate-1 deny is LIFTED. The operative sandbox gate is therefore gate 3, and the expected refusal reason for most PERMISSION_DENIAL activities in this library is 'noQualifyingGrant', NOT 'inactivePermission'. In production all three gates hold and the brief's characterisation is correct.
authority_model.how_to_interpret_activities: Where an activity's expected authority says a capability is 'registered active:false and granted to no Role', read it as: DENY in production by gate 1; in platform-sandbox, DENY by gate 3 unless the persona holds the qualifying Role. An executed activity that is refused should record WHICH reason the resolver returned — inactivePermission and noQualifyingGrant are different findings. An activity refused with inactivePermission in platform-sandbox would itself be a defect, because the environment override should have lifted that gate.

stories.title: The Tuesday supplier drop at Phoenix Main
stories.narrative_arc: A 14-carton pallet from the Taylor factory distributor lands on the Phoenix dock at 07:40. Ray works it from the handheld while Marisol watches the queue from her desk. By the end of the morning the pallet is receipted, one line is short, one barcode is lowercase, the dock Wi-Fi drops once, and a part arrives that the catalog knows about but the Part master does not.
stories.primary_surface: Receiving workspace — awaiting-receipt queue, supplier multi-scan session, handheld receipt lines
stories.why_this_story_exists: Receiving is where quantity enters the system. If the receipt posts but availability does not move, or moves by the wrong amount, every downstream promise is wrong. This story walks the single most repeated warehouse act in the company and checks the number at the end.

stories.title: A reorder request is born from a recommendation
stories.narrative_arc: The beater assemblies are down to two and a Sunburst franchise rebuild is on the schedule. The analytics panel raises a recommendation, Marisol turns it into a reorder request, and the request immediately inherits whatever the availability math believed.
stories.primary_surface: Operations → Inventory Health recommendations; reorder request creation
stories.why_this_story_exists: A reorder request is a purchasing commitment derived from a number. If the number is wrong the company buys the wrong quantity of the wrong part. This story attacks the derivation at its point of use.

stories.title: Review, approve, reject — the first handoff
stories.narrative_arc: Eight requests sit in PENDING_REVIEW. Hector works the queue: approves most, rejects one with a reason, tries to reject one without a reason, and discovers that approval hands ownership to a role rather than to a person.
stories.primary_surface: Reorder review queue — the PENDING_REVIEW allow-update branch in Firestore Rules
stories.why_this_story_exists: This is the first true role handoff in the procurement chain, and the whole transition is enforced in Rules rather than in a callable. Rules refusals are notoriously illegible to the operator.

stories.title: Assignment and the purchasing desk
stories.narrative_arc: An approved request sits owned by a ROLE. Marisol assigns it to Dwayne, who starts purchasing, calls the vendor twice, posts two updates, and goes home before the vendor calls back. The whole chain is assignee-restricted in Rules, which means every legitimate cover arrangement is a refusal.
stories.primary_surface: Reorder request detail — the Assign / Start Purchasing / Post Purchasing Update branches in Rules
stories.why_this_story_exists: Three consecutive transitions are gated on request.auth.uid == resource.data.assignedToUserId. That is correct governance and a real operational trap: the person who owns the request is the only person who can move it, and nothing in Rules reassigns it once purchasing has started.

stories.title: Recording the purchase order
stories.narrative_arc: Dwayne places the order with the vendor and records the PO. This is the one place in the whole reorder chain where a callable — not a Rules branch — owns the write, because two documents must land together or not at all. It is also where the three purchasing rulings become concrete: immutable PO, PO id == request id, and a void that writes a void record.
stories.primary_surface: Reorder request detail → Record purchase order; recordReorderPurchaseOrder callable
stories.why_this_story_exists: The Record-PO Rules branch was RETIRED and the invariant MOVED into an Admin-SDK transaction. That is a governance relocation, and relocations are where guarantees quietly go missing. These activities test that the guarantee actually moved.

stories.title: Voiding a purchase order
stories.narrative_arc: The vendor calls: the beater assemblies are discontinued and the order is dead. A PO cannot be edited or deleted, so the only lawful exit is a void — and the void is the most heavily guarded transition in the entire reorder state machine: double-gated on authority AND assignee, with a get() existence proof of the PO and an existsAfter() proof of the void record it creates.
stories.primary_surface: Reorder request detail → Void purchase order; the Void allow-update branch in Firestore Rules
stories.why_this_story_exists: Void writes a void RECORD — a ruling with teeth, enforced by a cross-document getAfter() invariant. Cross-document invariants in Rules are exactly the kind of guarantee that breaks silently when a client batch is reshaped, and the refusals they produce are the least legible in the system.

stories.title: Cancelling, and the states you cannot leave
stories.narrative_arc: Not every request becomes an order. Some are cancelled, some are rejected, and some reach a terminal state and stay there forever. This story maps the exits — and the places where there is no exit at all.
stories.primary_surface: Reorder request detail → Cancel; the Cancel allow-update branch and the terminal states
stories.why_this_story_exists: Cancel is reachable from exactly three pre-order statuses and is admin/dispatcher-only. Everything else is a dead end. Knowing which dead ends exist is the difference between a clean queue and a queue full of requests nobody can close.

stories.title: Mark received — the closeout that touches no stock
stories.narrative_arc: The beater assemblies arrive. Dwayne marks the request RECEIVED and the queue goes quiet. But the ORDERED -> RECEIVED transition is, by explicit design, a status-closeout note that writes NOTHING to inventory_transactions. The parts are on the dock and the ledger does not know. Closing that gap is on the architecture backlog, blocked on Firebase Blaze.
stories.primary_surface: Reorder request detail → Mark received; the ORDERED -> RECEIVED branch in Rules
stories.why_this_story_exists: This is the seam between purchasing and inventory, and today it is not joined. An operator who marks a request RECEIVED reasonably believes the stock is in the system. It is not. Every activity here is pointed at that belief.

stories.title: The number on the screen
stories.narrative_arc: Every promise this company makes — a dispatch, a sales order, a reorder recommendation — is made against one number in one column. That number is computed on the client by a function that adds a hardcoded 200-SKU baseline on top of ledger movement, ignores five of the nine operational movement types, and filters by neither location nor operating company. The server consolidated its own sign rule into one total function precisely because duplicates drift. This one was never folded in.
stories.primary_surface: Operations → Inventory Health; PartDetail; WarehouseManagerHome — all rendering computeAvailableStockByPart
stories.why_this_story_exists: This is the single richest defect surface in the inventory domain, and it is testable TODAY as a pure function with no emulator. Every activity here is an arithmetic assertion against a located line.

stories.title: Stock on a truck is not stock in the warehouse
stories.narrative_arc: Curt's TRK-14 carries about forty parts. They belong to the company, they are in the ledger, and the client availability derivation cannot tell them from warehouse stock because it filters by no location at all. So a dispatcher in Phoenix can promise a customer a gasket that is currently in a van on the I-10.
stories.primary_surface: Inventory Health and the dispatch path; the location field on inventory_transactions
stories.why_this_story_exists: The server explicitly excludes MOBILE/truck stock from committable warehouse stock and has a test for it. The client derivation has no location term whatsoever. That asymmetry is the story.

stories.title: Two companies, one shelf
stories.narrative_arc: Taylor and Ventana share an account base and, in practice, a building. Allocation is operating-company blind: a Ventana order can be promised against Taylor stock, silently. DECISIONS #165 ruling 4 says reservations must be attributable to operatingCompanyId AND an inventory location, and that company must not be inferred from location nor location from ownership. That ruling is NOT closed.
stories.primary_surface: Allocation and reservation paths; Inventory Health; the reservation ledger
stories.why_this_story_exists: Intercompany inventory that nobody can attribute is an audit finding and a tax problem, not just a UX gap. Every activity here is written to make the attribution either appear or be proven absent.

stories.title: The stock that was used and never left
stories.narrative_arc: DECISIONS #165 found a defect inside a ratified derivation: consumed stock never leaves on-hand. sumLedgerEligibleOnHand counts only physical movement types, legacy commitment rows carry no location, and consumeParts writes no physical removal — so a CONSUMED entry is invisible twice over. Two code paths compensate differently, and the ruling that would settle it was explicitly declined.
stories.primary_surface: Work-order consumption; the reservation ledger; availability on both paths
stories.why_this_story_exists: This is the one place in the inventory domain where the Owner looked at a disagreement and declined to rule. `RESERVED − RELEASED` versus `RESERVED − RELEASED − CONSUMED` is an open question with two live answers, and the arithmetic in DECISIONS #165 is explicit: 5 available after 5 received and 2 consumed, when 3 physically remain.

stories.title: Two hundred SKUs that are not parts
stories.narrative_arc: A hardcoded 200-SKU array lives in the client bundle. It is the only warehouseQty baseline the availability math has, its SKUs are not canonical, and client display paths still read it. Meanwhile the canonical Part master is a governed collection with its own identity rules that BLOCK the whole catalog on any ambiguity. Most operators do not know there are two.
stories.primary_surface: Parts list, Part detail, Part master list, Warehouse Manager home
stories.why_this_story_exists: Two sources of part identity, one of them checked into the client bundle, both rendered in the same columns. Every confusion in this library about 'what is this part' traces back here.

stories.title: Two parts, one part number
stories.narrative_arc: A Sunburst rebuild quote comes back with a beater motor line nobody can price, because TST-1022 exists twice in the Part master under two different document ids. Marisol works the identity problem from the Part Master workspace, Tessa works it from the import side, Luis keeps scanning labels that resolve to whichever record answered first, and by the afternoon everyone has learned that the 200-SKU static catalog on the screen is not the Part master at all.
stories.primary_surface: Part Master administration workspace, Parts catalog list, scanner alias lookup, inventory import preview
stories.why_this_story_exists: Part identity is the join key for every quantity in the company. If two Parts claim one internal part number, or one barcode claims two Parts, then every ledger row, every reservation and every reorder is attached to a coin flip. Two real defects of exactly this shape were fixed in Wave 1; this story is the regression suite that would catch them coming back.

stories.title: The bin registry that nobody can use
stories.narrative_arc: Priya has approved a racking project: label every aisle at Phoenix Main so a new hire can find a drive belt without asking. Sam Ortega opens Administration -> Warehouse Racking, generates a layout for aisle A, and discovers a complete, careful, well-tested bin registry sitting behind four capabilities that are registered active:false and granted to no Role. The screens are real. The commands are real. The sandbox has zero bins and no way to get one.
stories.primary_surface: Administration -> Warehouse Racking, Labels & Export, bin pickers on the scan surfaces
stories.why_this_story_exists: A shipped screen over an inert capability is worse than no screen: it teaches a user that a thing is possible and then refuses them at the last step, after the work is typed. This story walks the whole bin lifecycle — create, rename, retire, label — and checks whether each refusal is legible, or whether the surface just renders empty and lets the operator conclude the warehouse has no racking.

stories.title: Where did we put it?
stories.narrative_arc: A Desert Creamery rebuild is booked for Thursday and Dwayne has to stage nine parts for it. Ray has receipted them, Luis has to stow them, Curt has to find them on Thursday morning, and Priya wants a report at the end of the day saying the staging is done. Every one of those steps runs through put-away, which records a PLACE and deliberately records no BALANCE — and almost nobody using the screen knows that.
stories.primary_surface: Scan -> Put Away, bin placement history, offline warehouse intent queue
stories.why_this_story_exists: Put-away is the one inventory act in the system that is correct precisely because it does nothing to quantity. That design is load-bearing — if stowing a receipt removed it from sellable on-hand the whole company would break — and it is also the single most counter-intuitive thing on the warehouse surface. This story checks whether the screens say so, at the moment it matters, to the person it matters to.

stories.title: Moving stock across the aisle
stories.narrative_arc: Phoenix Main is converting from a warehouse-direct pile to binned racking. That means taking stock that the ledger records as sitting at WH-PHX-MAIN and re-stating it as sitting in bin A-14 of WH-PHX-MAIN — a RELOCATION_OUT at the warehouse and a RELOCATION_IN at the bin, signed to sum to zero. Tessa runs the conversion, Luis does the scanning, the Wi-Fi drops, one operator relocates across warehouses by mistake, and at month end Brenda checks that the pairs balance.
stories.primary_surface: Scan -> Move Stock (warehouse multi-scan), relocation reconciliation, month-end ledger review
stories.why_this_story_exists: Relocation is the only movement in the system whose entire job is to leave the total unchanged. That makes it the perfect test of whether the ledger's sign rule, the client's availability math and the reconciliation window agree with each other — and they demonstrably do not, because the client derivation has no RELOCATION term at all.

stories.title: Nobody has ever created a warehouse
stories.narrative_arc: Ventana is opening a second stocking location and Priya asks Sam to add it. Sam discovers that the governed warehouse writer exists, is careful, is tested, is unexported, has no callable and has no caller — every warehouse in the system arrived through a seed script or an operator CLI. Meanwhile Tessa is chasing why a Tucson opening-balance import refuses a warehouse by name, and Marisol keeps finding screens and metadata that still point at stock_locations, which the Owner retired tonight.
stories.primary_surface: Administration warehouse surfaces, warehouse metadata list views, inventory import preview, Operations warehouse panel
stories.why_this_story_exists: A warehouse record is the custody authority for every quantity in the company, and its ACTIVE/INACTIVE status decides where a balance may even be stated. If the only way to create or retire one is a script run by one person, then the most load-bearing master data in the system has no governed path, no audit trail a business user can read, and no owner inside the product.

stories.title: What a scan means
stories.narrative_arc: Luis runs the handheld through a normal Thursday of label reads at WH-PHX-MAIN, and by lunchtime he has scanned a clean part barcode, a lowercase reprint, a pair of codes that differ only by case, a machine serial plate, a bin label, a code nobody recognises, and a gasket carton whose label a forklift tyre tore in half. Tessa reviews the day's resolutions from her desk at 17:10 and finds she cannot tell, for any given ledger row, what the operator actually pointed the gun at.
stories.primary_surface: Handheld scanner identity surface — scannerPartLookup callable, client resolveScannedIdentity, part detail confirmation screen
stories.why_this_story_exists: A scan is not a fact, it is a guess about which record the operator meant. Every quantity in this system enters through one of these guesses. If resolution is silent, wrong, or unrecorded, the ledger stays internally consistent while describing the wrong parts, and nothing downstream can detect it.

stories.title: One receiving session, start to finish, on the gun
stories.narrative_arc: Ray opens a multi-scan receiving session against RCV-4488 at 08:05 on the Phoenix dock. Six lines in, he fat-fingers a quantity; nine lines in he realises line 3 went against the wrong part; at line 11 the yard calls him away for twenty minutes and he simply puts the gun down. Dwayne picks it up. The session closes at 09:50 and the availability panel on Marisol's desk disagrees with the ledger.
stories.primary_surface: Handheld receiving session — multi-scan line entry, session state, plus the desktop availability panel that reads the result
stories.why_this_story_exists: Receiving is the single most repeated warehouse act and the only routine way quantity enters the system. A session that cannot be corrected, abandoned, resumed or handed over will be worked around, and the workaround is always the same: write it on paper and fix it later. This story checks whether the number at the end matches the boxes.

stories.title: The gun in the freezer, the network in the parking lot
stories.narrative_arc: Luis counts gasket stock in the -10F walk-in at Phoenix Main where there is no signal at all, comes out to a Wi-Fi edge that drops every ninety seconds, retries a line he cannot tell landed, kills the handheld battery at 21:40 during a night count, hands the half-finished session to Owen at shift change, and leaves Tessa a reconciliation job for the morning.
stories.primary_surface: Handheld scanner under degraded connectivity — offline queue, retry, idempotency, session survival across device and operator
stories.why_this_story_exists: Every warehouse has a dead zone and every handheld has a battery. A system that only works on a good connection is a system that produces paper. The specific danger is a retry that lands twice against an append-only ledger, because the second copy can never be deleted.

stories.title: Who is allowed to scan what
stories.narrative_arc: Over one week the same barcode is pointed at by six different people: a field technician standing in the warehouse, a stocker holding a machine's serial plate, a Ventana technician in a Taylor building, a satellite attendant a hundred miles from his assigned location, an operations manager who only wants to look, and a system admin who is asked to make one of the refusals go away. Brenda reads the resulting denial log at month end and cannot tell a policy from a bug.
stories.primary_surface: Scanner authority surface — capability checks behind scanner actions, refusal rendering, Role administration desktop
stories.why_this_story_exists: A refusal is a piece of user interface. If it does not say what was refused, on whose behalf, and what the holder should do next, people route around it — they borrow a login, they write it on paper, or they call the one person whose Role does work and have them do it. Every one of those is worse than the refusal. The additional hazard here is that most inventory capabilities are registered inactive, so many of these refusals are not policy at all — they are absence wearing policy's clothes.

stories.title: Curt loads TRK-14 before the Tuesday run
stories.narrative_arc: 06:15 at Phoenix Main. Curt has six calls booked — two Sunburst DQ stores, Desert Creamery, Mesa Cinemas 18 and a pair of Circle K ice machines — and a truck that came back last night three beaters and a condenser motor lighter than it left. Marisol builds him a restock, Dwayne picks it, it gets dispatched, Curt receives it on the truck, and then the desktop availability panel still counts every one of those parts as sitting in the warehouse.
stories.primary_surface: Truck restock — mobile truck stock view, desktop transfer creation, pick and dispatch, mobile receipt, end-of-day reconciliation
stories.why_this_story_exists: A technician truck is a warehouse that drives. Every part on it is company stock that the books still own, sitting at a location the availability math does not know is different from a shelf. This story exists because the client's availability derivation has no location filter, which means the moment stock moves to a truck it becomes double-counted in every promise the company makes.

stories.title: Four drive belts cross the company line
stories.narrative_arc: Nadia at Ventana needs four TST-1010 drive belts for an El Rancho Market job on Thursday. Ventana's own warehouse has none; Phoenix Main has eleven. The belts are one building away and two sets of books away. By Friday the belts are fitted, one came back unused into the wrong warehouse, and Brenda is trying to work out which company owns what at month end.
stories.primary_surface: Cross-company transfer — Ventana request, Taylor dispatch, Ventana receipt, allocation, and month-end intercompany reconciliation
stories.why_this_story_exists: Two operating companies sharing one account base is the structural fact of this business. Inventory is where it hurts, because a part is a thing with one physical location and two possible owners, and the system currently infers one from the other. DECISIONS #165 ruling 4 says explicitly that company must not be inferred from location nor location from ownership, and it is NOT closed. Allocation is operating-company blind today: a Ventana order can be promised against Taylor stock silently.

stories.title: Transfers that do not arrive
stories.narrative_arc: Four transfers go wrong in four different ways over one fortnight: one is dispatched to WH-TUC-SAT on the 3rd and still shows IN_TRANSIT on the 9th; one arrives eight cartons light; one is cancelled after the van has already left; and one is aimed at TRK-22 on the day Alma's truck goes in for a transmission. Hector, Owen, Marisol and Brenda each meet a different half of the mess.
stories.primary_surface: Transfer exception handling — in-flight aging, receipt discrepancy, post-dispatch cancellation, invalid destination, month-end in-transit valuation
stories.why_this_story_exists: A transfer is the only inventory operation with a gap in the middle where stock belongs to no location. Everything that goes wrong with transfers goes wrong in that gap. All four inventory.transfer.* capabilities are registered active:false and granted to no Role, which means every exception path in this story is currently unbuilt — and the workaround for an unbuilt exception path is always an ADJUSTED movement that destroys the link between the two halves.

stories.title: The quarterly cycle count at Phoenix Main
stories.narrative_arc: Q3 closes in nine days, so Tessa builds the quarter's count list on Monday, Dwayne and Luis count twelve parts off the handheld across Tuesday morning, and Marisol disposes of each counted line Tuesday afternoon. Nothing dramatic happens: one line is dead-on, one is off by one, one needs a reason typed, and the sheet closes. The story exists to prove the ordinary path actually works end to end — that a count someone does is a count the warehouse number later reflects.
stories.primary_surface: Inventory → Cycle Counts sheet workspace (desktop) and the handheld count/scan session
stories.why_this_story_exists: A cycle count is the only governed mechanism EOS has for correcting inventory truth without pretending a physical movement happened. If the ordinary quarterly count cannot be scheduled, counted, submitted and disposed of by the people who actually do it, every other inventory number in this library is resting on nothing. This is the baseline the other seven stories deviate from.

stories.title: The shortage that was already accounted for
stories.narrative_arc: At 08:10 Curt Ballard closes a work order at Desert Creamery and consumes two TST-1009 Beater Assemblies from WH-PHX-MAIN. At 09:30 Tessa opens a cycle count line on the same part at the same location. The shelf holds three; the ledger's five movements net to five if you read them the wrong way. Everything that happens next — the variance, the materiality call, the reason, the ADJUSTED row — is arithmetic built on one function, and this story puts that function on trial.
stories.primary_surface: Cycle Counts sheet workspace, the handheld count session, and the Inventory Health read
stories.why_this_story_exists: The expected quantity is the only number in a cycle count that the counter cannot check. If it is wrong, the count manufactures a variance out of nothing and then posts a permanent ADJUSTED row to correct a shortage that never existed — subtracting the same physical units twice, forever, in an append-only ledger. This is the richest defect shape in the inventory system and it deserves its own story.

stories.title: Regression guards — the two cycle-count defects that were fixed
stories.narrative_arc: Two real defects were found and FIXED IN WAVE 1. First: a cycle-count line could be counted and disposed of twice and DOUBLE-POST to an append-only ledger, where nothing can ever be deleted. Second: a SERIAL line silently produced NO movement at all while cheerfully reporting RECONCILED. Both are closed. Every activity in this story is therefore a REGRESSION GUARD, written to fail loudly if either defect ever returns, and every one of them says so explicitly rather than pretending to discover the problem fresh.
stories.primary_surface: Cycle Counts sheet workspace, the handheld count session, and the inventory_transactions ledger
stories.why_this_story_exists: A fix without a guard is a fix with a shelf life. These two defects share the property that makes them worth permanent guards: both are SILENT. A double-post produces a plausible number and a permanent row; a missing serial movement produces a green RECONCILED badge over an untouched ledger. Neither throws, neither is visible in the UI, and both are unrecoverable in an append-only store. Guards are the only thing standing between the fix and its quiet reversal.

stories.title: The machine in the cage — serialized asset custody
stories.narrative_arc: Taylor Freezer took a used Taylor 8756 shake freezer back from a closed Sunburst DQ store two years ago. It has been in the Phoenix cage ever since, on no purchase order, in no system. This week Gil needs it on the books so it can be sold refurbished. Along the way four people ask 'where is it', three of them mean different things by 'it', and two of them type a serial number into a part field.
stories.primary_surface: Serialized asset acquire flow, the serialized assets read surface, and the mobile serialized section
stories.why_this_story_exists: A serialized unit is the only inventory object where identity and quantity are the same fact. Quantity stock answers 'how many'; a machine answers 'which one, and where is that one right now'. EOS models these with two different authorities that name their location field differently, and the place where they meet is where custody goes missing.

stories.title: The custody record must follow the metal
stories.narrative_arc: A new Taylor C712 leaves the Phoenix cage on Thursday morning, rides TRK-14 to Circle K – Chandler #4412, and is installed and running by noon. Six custody states pass in four hours. On Friday morning Tessa counts the cage and the registry still says the machine is in it.
stories.primary_surface: Serialized asset custody chain, the mobile truck inventory surface, and the install flow
stories.why_this_story_exists: Custody is the one inventory fact that cannot be inferred from anything else. A quantity can be recounted; a machine's history cannot be reconstructed after the fact. This story follows one unit through every handoff and asks, at each one, whether the record moved when the metal moved — and ends at an OPEN, deliberately unfixed gap where it demonstrably did not.

stories.title: 17:30 at Phoenix Main — what a warehouse lead closes out
stories.narrative_arc: Marisol has forty minutes between the last will-call and the alarm. Two count sheets are half done, a handheld is sitting in the charger with an abandoned session on it, TRK-14 and TRK-22 have not been reconciled, Owen is still working at the Tucson satellite, and somebody needs to know whether today's adjustments landed. None of it is dramatic. All of it is the difference between a branch that knows its stock tomorrow morning and one that does not.
stories.primary_surface: Cycle Counts workspace, Warehouse Manager home, truck inventory, and the mobile reconciliation section
stories.why_this_story_exists: End of day is where unfinished inventory work either gets named or gets forgotten. Every open sheet, uncommitted count and unreconciled truck is a claim about stock that nobody has checked. This story asks whether a warehouse lead can SEE that list at 17:30 — because if she cannot, tomorrow's promises are made against yesterday's guesses.

stories.title: Month end — the Controller's four numbers
stories.narrative_arc: It is the 3rd. Brenda Kowalski needs September's inventory position for two operating companies, and she needs it to be the same number in every place someone might look. She has an operational close that is a pure function nobody calls, a cost engine with no caller at all, a client availability figure that adds a static baseline to live movement, and two count sheets still open from the 30th.
stories.primary_surface: Finance close surfaces, inventory analytics, and the cycle count workspace at cut-off
stories.why_this_story_exists: A month-end inventory number has a property no operational number has: it is published, and people act on it for a year. Everything this library has found about divergent derivations, missing operating-company attribution and unfinished counts converges here, at the one moment when the difference between two plausible numbers becomes a difference between two sets of books.

stories.title: The opening-balance workbook
stories.narrative_arc: Ventana is being brought onto EOS. Sam and Gil have a 4,100-row spreadsheet exported from the old system: parts, warehouse names typed by a human, and an opening quantity for each. Two of the warehouse names are duplicated in the register, two parts share an Internal Part Number, and one column is a serial number in a quantity field. Every one of those rows is a permanent ledger write if the import chooses instead of refusing — which is exactly what two of them used to do.
stories.primary_surface: Data import intake, preview and execution, and the inventory ledger it writes into
stories.why_this_story_exists: An import is the highest-leverage write in the platform: one file, thousands of append-only rows, no undo. Two of its worst defects — a fuzzy warehouse name match and a coin-flip part lookup — were FIXED IN WAVE 1, and the fixes turned silent guesses into named refusals. This story guards those fixes and then follows a bad import downstream to show what the guards are protecting.

activities.title: Open the awaiting-receipt queue for the day
activities.starting_records_state: Three open supplier receipts exist for WH-PHX-MAIN; one belongs to ventana. No receipt lines recorded yet.
activities.business_purpose: Ray needs to know what is expected on the dock before he opens the first carton.
activities.preconditions: Ray holds an operational receiving Role. WH-PHX-MAIN is status ACTIVE.
activities.action: Open the Receiving workspace and read the awaiting-receipt queue.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: No transition. Read-only.
activities.expected_authority_capability: A receiving read capability. The queue must not show the ventana receipt to a taylor-scoped reader unless operating-company attribution is displayed on the row.
activities.expected_ui_result: Queue lists the taylor receipts with supplier name as the journey identity — the opaque order id must never render as the heading. A truthful LOADING/READY/EMPTY/DENIED state, not a silent empty list.
activities.expected_audit_result: A read. No audit row expected.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: None.
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: If the queue read fails it must say FAILED, not render EMPTY. An empty dock and a broken query must not look the same.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: The queue is three rows. A summary here is decoration.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ on the queue heading: what puts a receipt in this queue, and what removes it.
activities.reset_replay_notes: Read-only; no reset needed. Replay by reloading.
evidence: docs/design/north-star-migration-ledger.md:1735 — CURRENT: Frame 1a shipped one awaiting-receipt queue with a truthful LOADING/READY/EMPTY/DENIED/UNAVAILABLE/FAILED/PARTIAL ladder.

activities.title: Start the supplier multi-scan session

activities.business_purpose: Open one session so the whole pallet is receipted as one governed act rather than fourteen unrelated ones.

activities.action: Tap Start receiving session.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: Receipt moves from AWAITING to IN_PROGRESS for this operator.
activities.expected_authority_capability: A receiving session capability held by Ray's Role.
activities.expected_ui_result: Session header states the governed supplier name and explicitly states 'No order number recorded' rather than rendering a blank or an internal id.
activities.expected_audit_result: Session open recorded with operator identity and start time.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: None yet — no quantity has moved.
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: If a session is already open for this receipt under another operator, the second operator must be told who holds it, not silently given a parallel session.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: Opening a session is one tap.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ: what a session is for, and what happens to scanned lines if it is abandoned.
activities.reset_replay_notes: Reset: close or cancel the session. Replay needs the receipt returned to AWAITING.
evidence: docs/design/north-star-migration-ledger.md:1737 — CURRENT: the supplier multi-scan session states the missing order number rather than rendering receivingId.

activities.title: Scan and receipt 12 × TST-1007 Door Gasket - HD
activities.starting_records_state: Session open. TST-1007 has a canonical Part record and prior ledger history at WH-PHX-MAIN.
activities.business_purpose: Put twelve gaskets into governed stock so the service queue can be promised against them.
activities.preconditions: Carton label scans cleanly. Expected quantity on the receipt line is 12.
activities.action: Scan the carton barcode, confirm quantity 12, submit the line.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: A RECEIVED movement is appended to inventory_transactions for partId TST-1007, quantity 12, location { type: WAREHOUSE, locationId: WH-PHX-MAIN }, operatingCompanyId taylor. Append-only — no balance document is mutated.
activities.expected_authority_capability: A receiving/stock-receive capability. inventory.stock.receive is the registered capability for this act.
activities.expected_ui_result: Line shows as receipted with the quantity actually recorded, not the quantity expected.
activities.expected_audit_result: One immutable ledger row with operator identity, timestamp, receipt id and location.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: Warehouse on-hand at WH-PHX-MAIN rises by 12 under the server's MOVEMENT_SIGN rule (RECEIVED = PLUS).
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: If the write fails the line must remain unreceipted and rescannable. A half-written line is the worst outcome.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: Scanning a known barcode needs no model.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ on the quantity field: received quantity is what you physically have, not what the supplier claimed.

evidence: functions/src/inventoryLedger/operationalMovementTypes.ts:18-60 — CURRENT: the operational vocabulary is RECEIVED, RETURNED, TRANSFER_IN, TRANSFER_OUT, SCRAPPED, ADJUSTED, WORK_ORDER_CONSUMPTION, RELOCATION_OUT, RELOCATION_IN; LEGACY_TRANSACTION_TYPES (line 47) are RESERVED, RELEASED, CONSUMED.

functions/src/inventoryLedger/locationOnHand.ts:1-58 — CURRENT: the server's single TOTAL MOVEMENT_SIGN rule over the whole movement vocabulary, written precisely because the sign rule had been duplicated five times and only one copy learned about WORK_ORDER_CONSUMPTION. The client derivation above is a surviving sixth copy that was never folded in.
Firestore-emulator suites hang in this environment (port 8080 is an unrelated uvicorn), so the ledger write cannot be exercised here.

activities.title: Scan a carton whose printed barcode is lowercase
activities.starting_records_state: Carton for the beater assembly carries a reprinted label reading 'tst-1009' in lowercase. A canonical Part exists at document id TST-1009.
activities.business_purpose: Receipt the beater assemblies without putting a part Ray never chose into the ledger.
activities.preconditions: Session open. The lowercase code is what the scanner emits.
activities.action: Scan the lowercase barcode and accept whatever the screen offers.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: DESIRED: exactly one Part resolves, or the operator is asked to choose explicitly. A scan must never contribute two candidate document ids that differ only by case and have one of them silently win.
activities.expected_authority_capability: Scanner part-lookup read capability. Resolution is not an authority decision and must not be treated as one.
activities.expected_ui_result: The resolved part is shown with its canonical id and name for confirmation BEFORE the quantity is committed. If two candidates exist, both are shown.
activities.expected_audit_result: The ledger row must carry the partId the operator confirmed on screen, and the audit trail must record the raw scanned text alongside it.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: A wrong resolution here writes quantity against the wrong Part and silently corrupts availability for two SKUs.
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: If the operator realises the wrong part was resolved after committing, the correction path is a reversing movement, not an edit — and the UI must offer it.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: Ranking ambiguous scan candidates by recent receipt history is a genuine assist. Auto-selecting one without showing the operator is not.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ: why a scan can be ambiguous, and what to do when it is.
activities.reset_replay_notes: Replay by re-scanning; no state to reset if resolution is refused. If it commits, see A03's reset note.
evidence: functions/src/partMaster/scannerPartLookup.ts:9-10,79 — CURRENT: one scan contributes BOTH request.partCode and request.partCode.toUpperCase() as candidate document ids; the client's resolveScannedIdentity matches a Part code case-insensitively on partId.
This activity is written to FAIL if the upper-cased and raw candidate ids ever both resolve and one is chosen without operator confirmation. DESIRED behaviour is explicit disambiguation.

activities.title: Supplier shipped 10 of the 12 condenser fan motors
activities.starting_records_state: Receipt line for TST-1015 expects 12. Ten are physically on the pallet. No damage.
activities.business_purpose: Record what actually arrived, and leave a truthful open balance so the shortage is chased.

activities.expected_eos_state_transition: A RECEIVED movement of quantity 10 is appended. The receipt line becomes PARTIAL, not RECEIVED.
activities.expected_authority_capability: Same receive capability. Recording a short receipt is not a privileged act — it is the normal act.
activities.expected_ui_result: The line reads PARTIAL with the 2-unit shortfall stated in units, not as a percentage or a colour.
activities.expected_audit_result: Ledger row for 10. The variance of 2 is recorded against the receipt line, not the ledger.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: Availability rises by 10. A shortage follow-up should exist against the supplier — DESIRED; no capability in this repository creates one today.
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: If Ray later finds the missing two cartons behind the pallet, the recovery is a second RECEIVED movement on the same line, never an edit of the first.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: Drafting the shortage note to the supplier from the receipt line is real time saved.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ: what PARTIAL means for the open order, and who chases the shortfall.
activities.reset_replay_notes: Append-only ledger — same reset constraint as A03.
evidence: functions/src/inventoryLedger/operationalMovementTypes.ts:18-60 — CURRENT: the operational vocabulary is RECEIVED, RETURNED, TRANSFER_IN, TRANSFER_OUT, SCRAPPED, ADJUSTED, WORK_ORDER_CONSUMPTION, RELOCATION_OUT, RELOCATION_IN; LEGACY_TRANSACTION_TYPES (line 47) are RESERVED, RELEASED, CONSUMED.
DESIRED: a shortage follow-up object. No capability in functions/src creates one — mark MISSING_CAPABILITY if executed and none exists.

activities.title: Scan the same carton twice by accident
activities.starting_records_state: TST-1003 line already receipted at quantity 4 thirty seconds ago. Ray's thumb double-fires the trigger.
activities.business_purpose: Avoid inflating on-hand by four cylinders that do not exist.
activities.preconditions: Session open, line already committed once.
activities.action: Scan the identical carton barcode a second time and submit the same quantity.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: DESIRED: the second submission is recognised as a repeat of the same physical act and does NOT append a second RECEIVED row. CURRENT: an append-only ledger will happily hold both rows.
activities.expected_authority_capability: No additional authority. Idempotency is a correctness property, not a permission.
activities.expected_ui_result: The screen must say the line is already receipted and show the existing quantity — not present an empty quantity field that looks like a fresh line.
activities.expected_audit_result: At most one ledger row per physical receipt event. If a second row is written, the audit trail must make the duplication visible rather than burying it in a list.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: A duplicate RECEIVED row overstates availability by 4 cylinders — a part with a 4-week lead time.
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: Recovery from a committed duplicate is an ADJUSTED movement, which requires authority Ray may not hold. That escalation must be discoverable from the line.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: Flagging 'you scanned this 30 seconds ago' is cheap and useful.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ: why the system cannot simply delete the duplicate row.
activities.reset_replay_notes: Replay requires a fresh receipt. Reset is not possible on an append-only ledger.
evidence: functions/src/inventoryLedger/operationalMovementTypes.ts:18-60 — CURRENT: the operational vocabulary is RECEIVED, RETURNED, TRANSFER_IN, TRANSFER_OUT, SCRAPPED, ADJUSTED, WORK_ORDER_CONSUMPTION, RELOCATION_OUT, RELOCATION_IN; LEGACY_TRANSACTION_TYPES (line 47) are RESERVED, RELEASED, CONSUMED.
Written to FAIL if two identical RECEIVED rows can be produced from one carton with no idempotency key.

activities.title: Dock Wi-Fi drops mid-session
activities.starting_records_state: Six lines committed, one line submitted at the moment the access point at the roll-up door drops.
activities.business_purpose: Finish the pallet without losing six lines of work or double-posting the seventh.
activities.preconditions: Handheld loses connectivity for roughly 40 seconds while standing at the far bay.
activities.action: Submit a line, watch it hang, walk back into coverage, and retry the submission.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: DESIRED: the retried submission either completes the original write or is rejected as already-applied. Exactly one RECEIVED row exists for that line afterwards.
activities.expected_authority_capability: Unchanged.
activities.expected_ui_result: The handheld must distinguish 'not sent' from 'sent, result unknown'. Those need different words and different buttons.
activities.expected_audit_result: One ledger row. If the outcome is genuinely unknown, the audit trail must record the ambiguity rather than assert success.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: An unresolved in-flight write is how the same carton gets counted twice at the next cycle count.
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: This IS the recovery activity. The failure mode to catch is a Retry button that blindly re-posts.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: A model guessing whether the write landed is exactly the wrong tool. This needs an idempotency key, not an inference.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ: what 'result unknown' means and how to check before retrying.
activities.reset_replay_notes: Replay by throttling the network in devtools against the emulator. Reset needs a fresh dataset.
evidence: Emulator suites hang in this environment, and the handheld path needs a device or an emulated one. DESIRED: an idempotency key on the receipt-line write.

activities.title: A part arrives that the static catalog knows and the Part master does not

activities.title: The flush fires twice and eight becomes sixteen
activities.starting_records_state: The flush starts, the radio flaps once, and the device's retry logic resends the batch before the first response arrives.
activities.business_purpose: This is the single most expensive failure in the whole scanner story: duplicated quantity in an append-only ledger that can never be deleted, only offset by a correcting movement someone has to notice.
activities.preconditions: Eight lines in flight. No acknowledgement received. The device cannot distinguish 'never arrived' from 'arrived, response lost'.
activities.action: Let the retry fire.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: DESIRED: every queued line carries a client-generated idempotency key, and the server appends at most one movement per key. The second attempt returns the first attempt's result. CURRENT: no idempotency key is in evidence on the ledger write path, so a resend is indistinguishable from a second genuine carton.
activities.expected_authority_capability: Stock-receive. Idempotency is not an authority question, but its absence turns every authorised write into a potentially doubled one.
activities.expected_ui_result: DESIRED: the line list shows eight, never sixteen, regardless of how many times the batch was sent. CURRENT risk: sixteen units of TST-1007 on hand, with a perfectly clean audit trail of sixteen legitimate-looking RECEIVED rows.
activities.expected_audit_result: Sixteen immutable rows would each look correct in isolation. Nothing in the row says 'this is a resend'.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: On-hand overstates by eight. Availability overstates by eight. The next promise to Desert Creamery is made against stock that does not exist.
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: The only correction is an ADJUSTED -8 that somebody has to first notice is needed — which means a cycle count, weeks later, attributed to shrinkage.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: Detecting near-duplicate ledger rows (same part, same location, same quantity, seconds apart, same session) is a genuinely useful narrow detector and one of the few places a model would earn its place in this library — but it is a detector for a defect that should not exist.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ: why we never send the same scan twice, and what to do if you think we did.
activities.reset_replay_notes: No reset. Duplicated rows are permanent; replay requires a fresh dataset.

activities.title: The handheld battery dies at 21:40 during the night count
activities.starting_records_state: A scheduled after-hours count at WH-PHX-MAIN. Luis is nineteen lines into a session, four of them still in the offline queue from the freezer aisle. The battery hits zero and the device powers off hard.

activities.starting_records_state: 07:30. The night produced: fifteen acknowledged count lines under Luis, an unknown number under Owen, four lines stranded on a dead handheld, one possible duplicate from the retry in A05, and a -6 variance on TST-1016 that may or may not have moved the books.

activities.preconditions: Tessa holds an analyst Role at a desktop. All ledger rows are appended and immutable.
activities.action: Reconstruct the night: list every movement written between 20:00 and 00:00 at WH-PHX-MAIN, attribute each to an operator, and identify duplicates and gaps.

activities.title: End-of-day truck reconciliation at 18:20
activities.customer_account_context: TRK-14 — six calls across Sunburst DQ, Desert Creamery, Mesa Cinemas 18, Circle K – Chandler #4412
activities.starting_records_state: Six calls done. TRK-14 has four TRANSFER_IN rows from the morning and five WORK_ORDER_CONSUMPTION rows from the day. Curt reports what is physically left in the truck at shift end.
activities.business_purpose: Close the day honestly: what went on the truck, what got fitted, what is still rattling around in the back, and whether the system agrees with any of it.
activities.preconditions: Tessa holds an analyst Role. All rows are appended and immutable.
activities.action: Compare the server's exact on-hand for TRK-14 against Curt's physical report and against the availability panel.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: No transition. Read and compare.
activities.expected_authority_capability: CURRENT: inventory.balance.read is active:false, so there is no governed per-location balance surface to compare against. If executed, mark MISSING_CAPABILITY.
activities.expected_ui_result: DESIRED: three numbers that agree — server exact on-hand at TRK-14, the availability panel figure, and Curt's count. CURRENT: the availability panel is location-blind and omits WORK_ORDER_CONSUMPTION, so it will be high by exactly the day's consumption and will also be carrying warehouse stock in the same figure. The server's exact on-hand and Curt's count should match; the panel will not match either.
activities.expected_audit_result: The ledger holds the full movement history and is the only thing capable of settling the disagreement — and the daily reconciliation that would surface it is manual.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: Every open sales-order promise against these SKUs inherits the panel's error.

activities.title: Decide which side of the discrepancy writes the loss
activities.starting_records_state: The missing gasket from TRF-2231. Phoenix says eight went in the tote. Tucson says seven came out. Both are honest. One movement has to be written and it will be permanent.

activities.title: Open a line per part and snapshot the expected quantity blind
activities.starting_records_state: Sheet OPEN at WH-PHX-MAIN (assuming A02 was unblocked). No lines yet.
activities.business_purpose: Freeze what the system believes is on hand at the moment each line opens, so the count is measured against a number nobody can move afterwards.
activities.preconditions: Each chosen part resolves to a canonical Part with a tracking mode.
activities.action: Add twelve lines, one per part.
activities.expected_eos_state_transition: Each line goes (none) → OPEN with a server-computed expectedQuantity (NONE mode) or expectedSerialNumbers (SERIAL mode) stamped at its real instant and never recomputed.
activities.expected_authority_capability: inventory.cycleCount.create covers opening a line on a sheet.
activities.expected_ui_result: The expected value must NOT appear anywhere on screen for an OPEN line — the server does not even send it, so there is nothing in the client to leak.
activities.expected_audit_result: One audit event per line open, carrying the location, the part and the opening actor.
activities.expected_cross_object_effect: The snapshot reads the ledger through the ONE on-hand authority at the exact (part, location) pair, so a RELOCATION_OUT/RELOCATION_IN pair is counted exactly where it happened.
activities.exception_recovery_behaviour: If a part's Part record cannot be resolved the line must refuse by name, not open with a zero expected quantity. Zero and unknown are different facts and only one of them is safe to count against.
activities.ai_opportunity_note: Any model output that hints at the expected quantity destroys the blind property this whole design exists to protect.
activities.help_info_opportunity: ⓘ on the line list: 'Expected quantities are hidden until you submit this line. This is deliberate.'
activities.reset_replay_notes: Reset: cancel each line while OPEN. Once a line is submitted, cancellation is no longer available.
evidence: functions/src/cycleCount/cycleCountSheetCommand.ts:1-18,367-372 — CURRENT: schema v2, Decision #179 — one sheet per governed location, one line per Part, the expected snapshot server-computed when the LINE opens and never recomputed, BLIND until that line is submitted, and reconciliation one line per transaction so a sheet is resumable and never restartable. Each line's ledger key is ledgerKey(sheetId, partId, ...), so two lines cannot collide on one idempotency key.

functions/src/cycleCount/cycleCountExpectedQuantity.ts:50-59 — CURRENT: the expected quantity is `onHand += signedQuantity(v)` — the sign comes from inventoryLedger/locationOnHand.ts, the ONE place it is decided. The in-file comment records why: this line used to carry its own RECEIVED/TRANSFER/ADJUSTED branches and never learned WORK_ORDER_CONSUMPTION, so after Decision #171 made consumption live it counted consumed stock as still present — a count would 'find' the consumed quantity as a shortage, reconciliation would post an ADJUSTED for it, and the consumption would be subtracted twice.

functions/src/cycleCount/cycleCountExpectedQuantity.ts:37,49 — CURRENT: the transaction reads `where('partId','==',partId)` with NO operatingCompanyId predicate and NO location predicate, then filters location in memory by comparing BOTH location.type and location.locationId. Every ledger row for that part in both operating companies is pulled into the count transaction.

functions/src/inventoryLedger/locationOnHand.ts:19-31 — CURRENT: EXACT (sumExactLocationOnHand) never aggregates and is the only question a movement may ask of its source (Decision #170 Ruling 7); AGGREGATE (sumWarehouseAggregateOnHand) adds a warehouse's direct rows plus every child Bin's rows.
Firestore-emulator suites hang in this environment (port 8080 is an unrelated uvicorn), so the transactional snapshot cannot be exercised here.
